meaning: A friendly greeting meaning "How are you?" Usually you answer "Good, thanks, you?" rather than giving a long reply.
aussie: "How ya going?" — quick, relaxed, with "ya" and "going" linked together.
standard: "How are you doing?" — slower, with every word pronounced clearly.
mistake: Pronouncing every word separately and clearly. In casual Australian speech the words glide together and the ending of "going" is often softened.
tip: Say it as one smooth chunk of four beats. Put the strongest stress on GO.
examples: Good morning! How ya going today?

meaning: A casual greeting, short for "good day". It can be used at any time of day.
aussie: "G'day" — the second syllable has a wide, gliding vowel, and the first syllable is very short.
standard: "Good day" — two full words, with a clear D sound and a shorter vowel.
mistake: Stressing the first syllable. The stress is on the second part: guh-DAY.
tip: Make the first sound almost silent, then open your mouth wide and glide on the second syllable.

meaning: A relaxed way to say "You're welcome", "That's fine" or "Don't worry about it".
aussie: "No worries" — often said lightly and quickly, as a reply to thanks or an apology.
standard: "You're welcome" or "It's no problem" — more formal and less casual.
mistake: Saying it slowly and stressing both words equally sounds stiff. Put the stress on WOR and let the rest fall away.
tip: Think of it as two beats: noh-WUR-ries, with a soft ending.
examples: Thanks for your help! — No worries.
Can you send that today? — No worries.

meaning: A casual way to say "I think" or "I believe". Often used to give an opinion.
aussie: "I reckon it'll rain" — informal and very common in everyday speech.
standard: "I think it will rain" — neutral and a little more formal.
mistake: Pronouncing the last syllable as a full "con". It is a weak syllable, closer to "kn".
tip: Stress the first syllable of reckon: REK-n.
examples: I reckon we should leave now.
Do you reckon it's worth it?

meaning: How to order a flat white, a popular espresso coffee with steamed milk, at an Australian café.
aussie: "Flat white, please" — short and polite. You can add "to go" if you want it takeaway.
standard: "Could I please have a flat white?" — also fine, but slightly longer.
mistake: Over-explaining the order. A short, clear order is normal in Australian cafés.
examples: Can I get a large flat white to go?
A flat white and a banana bread, thanks.

meaning: A polite way to ask a real estate agent to arrange a time to view a rental property.
aussie: In Australia, an "inspection" is the usual word for viewing a rental property.
standard: In other countries people may say "viewing" or "showing".
mistake: Using "visit" or "see the house" when the agent expects "inspection".
tip: Link the first three words: kn-eye-BOOK. Stress SPEC in inspection.
examples: Can I book an inspection for Saturday?
Is there an inspection open this week?
I'd like to book an inspection, please.
